analysis.one_liner: Replaces state product-injury lawsuit rules with one federal standard that makes suing defective-product makers harder.
analysis.headline: After clearing a Senate committee in 1991, the bill never reached a floor vote: three procedural votes in September 1992 to open debate peaked at 58 of the 60 votes needed, and the bill died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have thrown out the patchwork of state product liability laws and replaced them with one federal rule for injury cases caused by defective products. It would have set a two-year deadline to sue, made punitive damages much harder to win, barred punitive damages entirely against FDA-approved drugs and devices and FAA-certified aircraft, made each defendant pay only its own share of pain-and-suffering awards, and reduced any award by the workers' compensation benefits the injured person receives. The practical effect would be fewer lawsuits against manufacturers and smaller recoveries for people hurt by dangerous products.
analysis.who_benefits: Manufacturers and sellers of products — especially drug makers, medical device makers, aircraft manufacturers, and the liability insurers that cover them — gain if the bill passes. They face a shorter window to be sued, a much higher bar for punitive damages, immunity from punitive damages for federally approved products, limits on suing mere sellers, and smaller payouts because awards are cut by workers' compensation benefits and each defendant pays only its own share.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Manufacturers, drug and aircraft makers, insurers

how_it_helps.text: A non-manufacturer product seller can be sued only if it failed to exercise reasonable care or made its own express warranty, sharply limiting claims against distributors and retailers [S2][S3].

Punitive damages are allowed only on clear and convincing evidence of 'conscious, flagrant indifference' to safety, and choosing a design with reasonable care can never qualify — far stricter than most state standards [S2][S3].

Punitive damages are barred against makers of FDA-approved drugs and medical devices and FAA-certified aircraft, unless the company withheld or misrepresented material information to the agency [S2][S3].
Suits must be filed within two years of discovering the harm, and claims about non-toxic harm from long-lived capital goods are barred 25 years after delivery [S2][S3].

Any damages award is reduced by the workers' compensation benefits the injured worker receives or is entitled to, and each defendant pays only its assigned share of noneconomic damages rather than the full judgment [S2][S3].
Intoxication can be a complete defense when the injured person was more than 50 percent responsible for the event [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: People injured by defective products bear the cost if the bill passes: shorter deadlines, a harder standard for punitive damages, awards reduced by workers' compensation benefits, and no way to collect pain-and-suffering damages from a defendant who cannot pay its share. State legislatures and courts also lose authority, since the federal standard overrides inconsistent state rules.

drawbacks.text: The two-year filing deadline would override longer deadlines some states allow, cutting off valid claims filed late even when the harm was slow to appear [S3].

The punitive damages shield covers FDA-approved drugs and FAA-certified aircraft even if the approved design later proves dangerous, leaving only the narrow exception for companies that misled the agency — removing a major deterrent to marketing products whose risks emerge after approval [S3].

Making liability for noneconomic damages 'several only' means that if one responsible defendant is insolvent or unidentified, the injured person absorbs the uncollected share of pain-and-suffering damages rather than the other defendants [S3].
Reducing damages by workers' compensation benefits shifts part of the cost of workplace injuries onto the injured worker and, ultimately, the workers' comp system instead of the product maker [S3].

Supporters' strongest argument was that fifty inconsistent state liability systems raised insurance costs, encouraged frivolous suits against deep-pocketed sellers, and deterred innovation — costs that eventually reach consumers in prices; the bill was the industry-side answer to that problem [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: There is a real, good-faith case that the state-by-state patchwork produced unpredictable outcomes and high liability costs, and some provisions (like protecting small sellers who could not inspect products) respond to genuine unfairness. But the bill's core effect moves risk from manufacturers to injured people: a stricter punitive standard plus near-immunity for federally approved drugs and aircraft, a hard two-year deadline, offsets for workers' comp, and no joint liability. The drug and aircraft shields in particular would have removed the main private enforcement check on products whose dangers surface after approval. On balance it is a substantial transfer of legal protection away from consumers.

outcome.mechanism: Supporters never got the Senate to open debate: three procedural votes in September 1992 topped out at 58 of the 60 votes needed to cut off a filibuster of the motion to proceed, so the bill never came to a floor vote and died when the 102nd Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Kasten introduced the bill on March 13, 1991 with 30 original cosponsors from both parties, and it was referred to the Commerce Committee [S1][S3].

The Commerce Committee held hearings in September 1991 and reported the bill favorably without amendment on November 14, 1991, with additional and minority views filed; it was placed on the Senate calendar [S5].
In June 1992 the bill was sent to the Judiciary Committee for hearings, which were held in August 1992; the committee was then discharged and the bill returned to the calendar [S5].

On September 10, 1992, cloture on the motion to proceed failed 57-39, was reconsidered and failed again 57-39, and failed a third time 58-38 — each short of the 60 votes needed to begin debate [S6][S7][S8].
The Senate never debated or voted on the bill's merits, the House never considered it, and it expired when the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Injured consumers and the plaintiffs' trial bar are better off because the bill died: state-law rights to sue product makers, including the ability to seek punitive damages against drug and aircraft manufacturers, were left intact. Manufacturers and their insurers did not get the shorter deadlines and damage limits they sought, and 35 Senate Democrats who opposed the bill kept it off the floor.

for.name: Sen. Robert Kasten
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Product Liability Fairness Act and recruited 30 original cosponsors across both parties.

for.name: 31 of 43 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; nearly all Republicans present voted to open debate on it.

for.name: 8 of 56 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Senator Rockefeller of West Virginia and Senator Lieberman of Connecticut; 18 Democrats voted to open debate.

for.name: Sen. Ernest Hollings
for.what_they_did: Held hearings in his committee and reported the bill favorably without amendment in November 1991.

against.name: 35 of 56 Senate Democrats
against.what_they_did: Voted no on all three cloture votes on the motion to proceed, keeping the bill from ever reaching the floor for a debate or vote.

against.name: Plaintiffs' trial lawyers and consumer groups
against.what_they_did: Opposed the bill in committee hearings and publicly as an industry-backed takeover of state product liability law; opposition was concentrated in the Democratic caucus.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's support was bipartisan on paper (39 cosponsors, including 8 Democrats), but the blocking votes split by party: 39 of 43 Republicans voted to open debate while only 18 of 56 Democrats did, leaving all three cloture votes short of the 60 needed.

industries.note: The bill would bar punitive damages against makers of FDA-approved drugs and devices, even when an approved product later proves dangerous, unless the company misled the agency. That removes the most powerful private deterrent against marketing drugs whose risks emerge after approval.

FAA-certified aircraft would be immune from punitive damages as long as the maker met certification and continuing-airworthiness obligations, with a narrow exception for withheld information. This would sharply cut exposure in aviation crash litigation.

A uniform two-year filing deadline, a stricter punitive damages standard, offsets for workers' compensation, and several liability all reduce the size and number of claims against manufacturers. The savings come out of compensation for injured consumers.
Fewer claims, shorter exposure windows, and caps on punitive and noneconomic recovery directly reduce payouts on product liability policies.

industries.industry: Distributors, retailers and other product sellers
industries.note: Non-manufacturer sellers could be sued only for their own carelessness or their own express warranty, shielding retailers and distributors from strict liability for products they did not make.

Harder standards, shorter deadlines, fee-shifting settlement rules, and mandatory alternative dispute resolution would shrink the volume and value of product liability cases the plaintiffs' bar can bring. Its interest here runs with injured consumers' ability to sue.
